verses.zh: 当三十年四月初五日，以西结（原文是我）在迦巴鲁河边被掳的人中，天就开了，得见　神的异象。
verses.en: In the thirtieth year,[NOTE:1] on the fifth day of the fourth month, while I was among the exiles[NOTE:2] at the Kebar River,[NOTE:3] the heavens opened[NOTE:4] and I saw a divine vision.[NOTE:5]
notes: The meaning of the thirtieth year is problematic. Some take it to mean the age of Ezekiel when he prophesied (e.g., Origen). The Aramaic Targum explains the thirtieth year as the thirtieth year dated from the recovery of the book of the Torah in the temple in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 22:3-9). The number seems somehow to be equated with the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s exile in 1:2, i.e., 593 b.c.

The Assyrians started the tactic of deportation, the large-scale forced displacement of conquered populations, in order to stifle rebellions. The task of uniting groups of deportees, gaining freedom from one’s overlords, and returning to retake one’s own country would be considerably more complicated than living in one’s homeland and waiting for an opportune moment to drive out the enemy’s soldiers. The Babylonians adopted this practice also, after defeating the Assyrians. The Babylonians deported Judeans on three occasions. The practice of deportation was reversed by the Persian conquerors of Babylon, who gained favor from their subjects by allowing them to return to their homeland. As polytheists, the Persians sought the favor of the gods of the various countries that had come under their control.
The Kebar River is mentioned in Babylonian texts from the city of Nippur in the fifth century b.c. It provided artificial irrigation from the Euphrates.
For the concept of the heavens opened in later literature, see 3 Macc 6:18; 2 Bar. 22:1; T. Levi 5:1; Matt 3:16; Acts 7:56; Rev 19:11.
Or “saw visions from God.” References to divine visions occur also in Ezek 8:3 and 40:2.

verses.zh: 正是约雅斤王被掳去第五年四月初五日，
verses.en: (On the fifth day of the month—it was the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s exile—

verses.zh: 在迦勒底人之地、迦巴鲁河边，耶和华的话特特临到布西的儿子祭司以西结；耶和华的灵（原文是手）降在他身上。
verses.en: the Lord’s message came to the priest Ezekiel[NOTE:1] the son of Buzi,[NOTE:2] at the Kebar River in the land of the Babylonians.[NOTE:3] The hand[NOTE:4] of the Lord came on him there.)
notes: The prophet’s name, Ezekiel, means in Hebrew “May God strengthen.”
Or “to Ezekiel son of Buzi the priest.”

Heb “Chaldeans.” The name of the tribal group ruling Babylon, “Chaldeans” is used as metonymy for the whole empire of Babylon. The Babylonians worked with the Medes to destroy the Assyrian Empire near the end of the 7th century b.c. Then, over the next century, the Babylonians dominated the West Semitic states (such as Phoenicia, Aram, Moab, Edom, and Judah in the modern countries of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, and Israel) and made incursions into Egypt.

Or “power.” sn Hand in the OT can refer metaphorically to power, authority, or influence. In Ezekiel God’s “hand” being on the prophet is regularly associated with communication or a vision from God (3:14, 22; 8:1; 37:1; 40:1).

verses.zh: 我观看，见狂风从北方刮来，随着有一朵包括闪烁火的大云，周围有光辉；从其中的火内发出好像光耀的精金；
verses.en: As I watched, I noticed[NOTE:1] a windstorm[NOTE:2] coming from the north—an enormous cloud, with lightning flashing,[NOTE:3] such that bright light[NOTE:4] rimmed it and came from[NOTE:5] it like glowing amber[NOTE:6] from the middle of a fire.
notes: The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) indicates becoming aware of something and has been translated here as a verb.
Storms are often associated with appearances of God (see Nah 1:3; Ps 18:12). In some passages, the “storm” (סְעָרָה, seʿarah) may be a whirlwind (Job 38:1; 2 Kgs 2:1).

Heb “fire taking hold of itself,” perhaps repeatedly. The phrase occurs elsewhere only in Exod 9:24 in association with a hailstorm. The LXX interprets the phrase as fire flashing like lightning, but it is possibly a self-sustaining blaze of divine origin. The LXX also reverses the order of the descriptors, i.e., “light went around it, and fire flashed like lightning within it.”
Or “radiance.” The term also occurs in 1:27b.
Or “was in it”; cf. LXX ἐν τῷ μέσῳ αὐτοῦ (en tō mesō autou, “in its midst”).
The LXX translates חַשְׁמַל (khashmal) with the word ἤλεκτρον (ēlektron, “electrum”; so NAB), an alloy of silver and gold, perhaps envisioning a comparison to the glow of molten metal.

verses.zh: 又从其中显出四个活物的形像来。他们的形状是这样：有人的形像，
verses.en: In the fire[NOTE:1] were what looked like[NOTE:2] four living beings.[NOTE:3] In their appearance they had human form,[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “from its midst” (מִתּוֹכָהּ, mitokhah). The LXX reads ἐν τῷ μέσῳ (en tō mesō, “in the midst of it”). The LXX also reads ἐν for מִתּוֹךְ (mitokh) in v. 4. The translator of the LXX of Ezekiel either read בְּתוֹךְ (betokh, “within”) in his Hebrew exemplar or could not imagine how מִתּוֹךְ could make sense and so chose to use ἐν. The Hebrew would be understood by adding “from its midst emerged the forms of four living beings.”
Heb “form, figure, appearance.”

The Hebrew term is feminine plural, yet thirty-three of the forty-five pronominal suffixes and verbal references that refer to the living beings in the chapter are masculine plural. The grammatical vacillation between masculine and feminine plurals suggests the difficulty Ezekiel had in penning these words as he was overcome by the vision of God. In ancient Near-Eastern sculpture very similar images of part-human, part-animal creatures serve as throne and sky bearers. For a discussion of ancient Near-Eastern parallels, see L. C. Allen, Ezekiel (WBC), 1:26-31. Ezekiel’s vision is an example of contextualization, where God accommodates his self-revelation to cultural expectations and norms.
They had human form may mean they stood erect.

verses.zh: 各有四个脸面，四个翅膀。
verses.en: but each had four faces and four wings.

verses.zh: 他们的腿是直的，脚掌好像牛犊之蹄，都灿烂如光明的铜。
verses.en: Their legs were straight, but the soles of their feet were like calves’ feet. They gleamed[NOTE:1] like polished bronze.
notes: The Hebrew verb translated gleamed occurs only here in the OT.

verses.zh: 在四面的翅膀以下有人的手。这四个活物的脸和翅膀乃是这样：
verses.en: They had human hands[NOTE:1] under their wings on their four sides. As for the faces and wings of the four of them,
notes: The MT reads “his hand” while many Hebrew mss as well as the Qere read “hands of.” Two similar Hebrew letters, vav and yod, have been confused.

verses.zh: 翅膀彼此相接，行走并不转身，俱各直往前行。
verses.en: their wings touched each other; they did not turn as they moved, but went straight ahead.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “They each went in the direction of one of his faces.”

verses.zh: 至于脸的形像：前面各有人的脸，右面各有狮子的脸，左面各有牛的脸，后面各有鹰的脸。
verses.en: Their faces had this appearance: Each of the four had the face of a man, with the face of a lion on the right, the face of an ox on the left, and also the face of an eagle.[NOTE:1]
notes: The MT has an additional word at the beginning of v. 11, וּפְנֵיהֶם (ufenehem, “and their faces”), which is missing from the LXX. As the rest of the verse only applies to wings, “their faces” would have to somehow be understood in the previous clause. But this would be very awkward and is doubly problematic since “their faces” are already introduced as the topic at the beginning of v. 10. The Hebrew scribe appears to have copied the phrase “and their faces and their wings” from v. 8, where it introduces the content of 9-11. Only “and (as for) their wings” belongs here.

verses.zh: 各展开上边的两个翅膀相接，各以下边的两个翅膀遮体。
verses.en: Their wings were spread out above them; each had two wings touching the wings of one of the other beings on either side and two wings covering their bodies.

verses.zh: 他们俱各直往前行。灵往哪里去，他们就往那里去，行走并不转身。
verses.en: Each moved straight ahead[NOTE:1]—wherever the spirit[NOTE:2] would go, they would go, without turning as they went.
notes: See the note on “straight ahead” in v. 9.
Or “wind.”

verses.zh: 至于四活物的形像，就如烧着火炭的形状，又如火把的形状。火在四活物中间上去下来，这火有光辉，从火中发出闪电。
verses.en: In the middle[NOTE:1] of the living beings was something like[NOTE:2] burning coals of fire[NOTE:3] or like torches. It moved back and forth among the living beings. It was bright, and lightning was flashing out of the fire.
notes: The MT reads: “and the form of the creatures” (וּדְמוּת הַחַיּוֹת, udemut hakhayyot). The LXX reads: “and in the midst of the creatures,” suggesting an underlying Hebrew text of וּמִתּוֹךְ הַחַיּוֹת (umittokh hakhayyot). The subsequent description of something moving among the creatures supports the LXX.

The MT reads: “and the form of the creatures—their appearance was like burning coals of fire.” The LXX reads: “in the midst of the creatures was a sight like burning coals of fire.” The MT may have adjusted “appearance” to “their appearance” to fit their reading of the beginning of the verse (see the note on “in the middle”). See M. Greenberg, Ezekiel (AB), 1:46.
Burning coals of fire are also a part of David’s poetic description of God’s appearance (see 2 Sam 22:9, 13; Ps 18:8).

verses.zh: 这活物往来奔走，好像电光一闪。
verses.en: The living beings moved backward and forward as quickly as flashes of lightning.[NOTE:1]
notes: The LXX omits v. 14 and may well be correct. The verse may be a later explanatory gloss of the end of v. 13 which was copied into the main text. See M. Greenberg, Ezekiel (AB), 1:46.tn Lit., “like the appearance of lightning.” The Hebrew term translated “lightning” occurs only here in the OT. In postbiblical Hebrew the term refers to a lightning flash.

verses.zh: 我正观看活物的时候，见活物的脸旁各有一轮在地上。
verses.en: Then I looked,[NOTE:1] and I saw one wheel[NOTE:2] on the ground[NOTE:3] beside each of the four beings.
notes: The MT includes “at the living beings,” which is absent from the LXX.
Another vision that includes wheels on thrones occurs in Dan 7:9. Ezekiel 10 contains a vision similar to this one.
The Hebrew word may be translated either “earth” or “ground” in this context.

verses.zh: 轮的形状和颜色（原文是作法）好像水苍玉。四轮都是一个样式，形状和作法好像轮中套轮。
verses.en: The appearance of the wheels and their construction[NOTE:1] was like gleaming jasper,[NOTE:2] and all four wheels looked alike. Their structure was like a wheel within a wheel.[NOTE:3]
notes: This word is omitted from the LXX.
Heb “Tarshish stone.” The meaning of this term is uncertain. The term has also been translated “topaz” (NEB, NIV11), “beryl” (KJV, NASB, NRSV), or “chrysolite” (RSV, NIV84).

Or “like a wheel at right angles to another wheel.” Some envision concentric wheels here, while others propose “a globe-like structure in which two wheels stand at right angles” (L. C. Allen, Ezekiel [WBC], 1:33-34). The description given in v. 17 favors the latter idea.

verses.zh: 轮行走的时候，向四方都能直行，并不掉转。
verses.en: When they moved they would go in any of the four directions they faced without turning as they moved.

verses.zh: 至于轮辋，高而可畏；四个轮辋周围满有眼睛。
verses.en: Their rims were high and awesome,[NOTE:1] and the rims of all four wheels were full of eyes all around.
notes: The MT reads וְיִרְאָה לָהֶם (veyirʾah lahem, “and fear belonged to them”). In a similar vision in 10:12 the wheels are described as having spokes (יְדֵיהֶם, yedehem). That parallel would suggest יָדוֹת (yadot) here (written יָדֹת without the mater lectionis). By positing both a ד/ר (dalet/resh) confusion and a ה/ת (hey/tav) confusion, the form was read as וְיָרֵה (veyareh) and was then misunderstood and subsequently written as וְיִרְאָה (veyirʾah) in the MT. The reading וְיִרְאָה does not seem to fit the context well, though in English it can be made to sound as if it does. See W. H. Brownlee, Ezekiel 1-19 (WBC), 8-9. The LXX reads καὶ εἶδον αὐτά (kai eidon auta, “and I saw”), which assumes וָאֵרֶא (vaʾereʾ). The existing consonants of the MT may also be read as “it was visible to them.”

verses.zh: 活物行走，轮也在旁边行走；活物从地上升，轮也都上升。
verses.en: When the living beings moved, the wheels beside them moved; when the living beings rose up from the ground, the wheels rose up too.

verses.zh: 灵往哪里去，活物就往那里去；活物上升，轮也在活物旁边上升，因为活物的灵在轮中。
verses.en: Wherever the spirit[NOTE:1] would go, they would go,[NOTE:2] and the wheels would rise up beside them because the spirit[NOTE:3] of the living being was in the wheel.
notes: Or “wind”; the same Hebrew word can be translated as either “wind” or “spirit,” depending on the context.
The MT includes the additional phrase “the spirit would go,” which seems unduly redundant here and may be dittographic.

Or “wind.” The Hebrew is difficult since the text presents four creatures and then talks about “the spirit” (singular) of “the living being” (singular). According to M. Greenberg (Ezekiel [AB], 1:45) the Targum interprets this as “will.” Greenberg views this as the spirit of the one enthroned above the creatures, but one would not expect the article when the one enthroned has not yet been introduced.

verses.zh: 那些行走，这些也行走；那些站住，这些也站住；那些从地上升，轮也在旁边上升，因为活物的灵在轮中。
verses.en: When the living beings moved, the wheels moved, and when they stopped moving, the wheels stopped.[NOTE:1] When they rose up from the ground, the wheels rose up from the ground; the wheels rose up beside them because the spirit of the living being was in the wheel.
notes: The LXX reads: “when it went, they went; when it stood, they stood.”tn Heb “when they went, they went; when they stood, they stood.”

verses.zh: 活物的头以上有穹苍的形像，看着像可畏的水晶，铺张在活物的头以上。
verses.en: Over the heads of the living beings was something like a platform,[NOTE:1] glittering awesomely like ice,[NOTE:2] stretched out over their heads.
notes: Or “like a dome” (NCV, NRSV, TEV).
Or “like crystal” (NRSV, NLT).

verses.zh: 穹苍以下，活物的翅膀直张，彼此相对；每活物有两个翅膀遮体。
verses.en: Under the platform their wings were stretched out, each toward the other. Each of the beings also had two wings covering[NOTE:1] its body.
notes: Heb “each had two wings covering and each had two wings covering,” a case of dittography. On the analogy of v. 11 and the support of the LXX, which reads the same for v. 11 and this verse, one should perhaps read “each had two wings touching another being and each had two wings covering.”

verses.zh: 活物行走的时候，我听见翅膀的响声，像大水的声音，像全能者的声音，也像军队哄嚷的声音。活物站住的时候，便将翅膀垂下。
verses.en: When they moved, I heard the sound of their wings—it was like the sound of rushing waters, or the voice of the Sovereign One,[NOTE:1] or the tumult[NOTE:2] of an army. When they stood still, they lowered their wings.
notes: Heb “Shaddai” (probably meaning “one of the mountain”), a title that depicts God as the sovereign ruler of the world who dispenses justice. The Old Greek translation omitted the phrase “voice of the Sovereign One.”
The only other occurrence of the Hebrew word translated “tumult” is in Jer 11:16. It indicates a noise like that of the turmoil of a military camp or the sound of an army on the march.

verses.zh: 在他们头以上的穹苍之上有声音。他们站住的时候，便将翅膀垂下。
verses.en: Then there was a voice from above the platform over their heads when they stood still.[NOTE:1]
notes: The MT continues: “when they stood still, they lowered their wings,” an apparent dittography from the end of v. 24. The LXX commits haplography by homoioteleuton, leaving out vv. 25b and 26a by skipping from רֹאשָׁם (roʾsham, “their head”) in v. 25 to רֹאשָׁם in v. 26.

verses.zh: 在他们头以上的穹苍之上有宝座的形像，彷佛蓝宝石；在宝座形像以上有彷佛人的形状。
verses.en: Above the platform over their heads was something like a sapphire shaped like a throne. High above on the throne was a form that appeared to be a man.

verses.zh: 我见从他腰以上有彷佛光耀的精金，周围都有火的形状，又见从他腰以下有彷佛火的形状，周围也有光辉。
verses.en: I saw an amber glow[NOTE:1] like a fire enclosed all around[NOTE:2] from his waist up. From his waist down I saw something that looked like fire. There was a brilliant light around it,
notes: See Ezek 1:4.

The LXX lacks this phrase. Its absence from the LXX may be explained as a case of haplography resulting from homoioteleuton, skipping from כְּמַרְאֵה (kemarʾeh) to מִמַּרְאֵה (mimmarʾeh). On the other hand, the LXX presents a much more balanced verse structure when it is recognized that the final words of this verse belong in the next sentence.

verses.zh: 下雨的日子，云中虹的形状怎样，周围光辉的形状也是怎样。这就是耶和华荣耀的形像。我一看见就俯伏在地，又听见一位说话的声音。
verses.en: like the appearance of a rainbow in the clouds after the rain.[NOTE:1] This was the appearance of the surrounding brilliant light; it looked like the glory of the Lord. When I saw[NOTE:2] it, I threw myself face down, and I heard a voice speaking.
notes: Reference to the glowing substance and the brilliant light and storm phenomena in vv. 27-28a echoes in reverse order the occurrence of these phenomena in v. 4.
The vision closes with the repetition of the verb “I saw” from the beginning of the vision in 1:4.
